title: Topics in Causal Inference
text:
Course description
This course explores modern topics in causal inference with a focus on randomized experiments and experimental design. The course develops the potential outcomes framework and builds toward advanced topics including covariate balancing, overlap conditions and positivity violations, causal inference under interference, and policy evaluation. The emphasis is on both theoretical foundations and applied practice. Causal inference from observational data is de-emphasized. Students will complete presentation and project work including both applied and theoretical replication studies.

title: How These Notes Are Made
text:
What guides a lecture
These lecture notes for the Yale S&DS graduate course “Topics in Causal Inference” are being developed through an instructor-directed, AI-assisted workflow. This page describes the generation process.
Every lecture begins with a public brief.md, written by me. The brief is a concise content outline: it records the lecture’s scope and emphases, a minimal literature list, and any examples, demonstrations, constraints, or open questions I choose to specify. It does not prescribe the section structure of the finished notes or pre-write assessments of the cited literature. For transparency, each lecture page links to the exact brief associated with that lecture.
Each lecture folder begins with only two files: the brief and a canonical index.qmd containing the lecture page. Assets are added only when the lecture actually needs them.
The brief is not the only instruction supplied during drafting. Four course-wide documents establish shared expectations:
These public files expose the durable course-specific instructions. They do not reproduce the model provider’s system instructions or chain of thought during drafting. The current plan uses GPT 5.6 Sol (Extra High), with plans to experiment with the possible benefits of 5.6 Sol (Pro).

title: How These Notes Are Made
text:
Drafting and revision process
The intended workflow is:

Scope. The instructor drafts a concise content outline and addresses lecture-specific scope, emphasis, and constraints.
Literature. The brief retains concise citations rather than extensive source commentary. Bibliographic details and technical claims are checked rather than inferred from memory. Primary papers are preferred for foundational claims and historical attributions; reviews and textbooks are used selectively when their synthesis or clarification is especially useful. Historical background and additional pointers that would interrupt the main lecture path are collected in a concise Further reading section.
Initial generation. OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol, normally in either the Extra High or Pro configuration, writes an initial version directly into the lecture’s index.qmd. Its metadata records the model and date and sets generation-locked: true. This flag prevents accidental wholesale regeneration; it does not make the file read-only. The model and configuration may change as the course develops, and the metadata will identify the system actually used.
Brief-driven iteration. During early drafting, the instructor may review the result, revise the brief, and explicitly request another full generation. That request temporarily clears the generation lock; the newly generated version is then locked again. A changed brief by itself never overwrites lecture text.
Instructor revision. Once the lecture’s structure is satisfactory, the instructor edits the canonical lecture file directly and may substantially revise the generated material. After those edits begin, revisions are targeted so that instructor-authored text is not overwritten.
Publication. Quarto renders the same source to a web page and to PDF. Interactive web demonstrations are checked alongside their static PDF fallbacks.

title: L01: Introduction
text:
A course about choices
Download: Lecture PDF
Causal inference begins with a comparison: what would happen under one course of action rather than another? Data do not answer that question on their own. We must decide what comparison matters, how treatment will be assigned, and how the resulting observations will be analyzed.
This course emphasizes design-based inference. We will treat the units and their potential outcomes as fixed and locate randomness in an assignment mechanism that we know because we chose it. That perspective keeps two kinds of choices visibly separate:
The causal target—the estimand—usually comes first and remains fixed while we compare designs and analyses. Sometimes the target itself changes. Trimming units with poor overlap in L04, for example, may improve the statistical problem by changing the population about which we ask the question. That is not merely a better estimator of the old target.
This distinction is a recurring discipline: what is the question, what was randomized, and what was calculated?

title: L01: Introduction
text:
Complete randomization
Under complete randomization, the experimenter fixes the treated count \(N_1\) in advance and therefore also fixes the control count \(N_0=N-N_1\). Assume \(0<N_1<N\), so both arms are nonempty. Every vector containing exactly \(N_1\) ones is equally likely:
\[
\mathbb P_Z(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z)
=
\begin{cases}
\binom{N}{N_1}^{-1}, & \sum_{i=1}^N z_i=N_1,\\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
There are \(\binom{N}{N_1}\) ways to choose the treated units, which explains the probability in the first line. Each unit has marginal treatment probability \(N_1/N\), but the assignments are not independent. If one unit is treated, one fewer treatment slot remains. In fact, for \(i\ne j\),
\[
\mathbb E_Z(Z_iZ_j)
=\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=1,Z_j=1)
=\frac{N_1(N_1-1)}{N(N-1)},
\]
and therefore
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_Z(Z_i,Z_j)
=-\frac{(N_1/N)(N_0/N)}{N-1}.
\]
That weak negative dependence is precisely what fixes the arm sizes.

title: L01: Introduction
text:
Bernoulli randomization
Under an independent Bernoulli design with common probability \(p\),
\[
Z_i\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),
\qquad
\mathbb P_Z(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z)
=p^{\sum_i z_i}(1-p)^{N-\sum_i z_i}.
\]
Now each unit receives an independent random draw, so the treated count \(N_1=\sum_iZ_i\) is random rather than fixed by the design. Throughout the course, \(N_1\) and \(N_0\) denote realized arm sizes: under complete randomization their values are fixed in advance, while under Bernoulli randomization they vary across possible assignments. The Bernoulli design is operationally simple and sometimes convenient for sequential enrollment. It can also produce imbalance. The probability of an empty treatment arm is \((1-p)^N\), and the probability of an empty control arm is \(p^N\). We return to that complication in L02.






NoteDesign comes before positivity



Write \(\pi_i=\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=1)\) for unit \(i\)’s marginal treatment probability. Positivity is a property of the assignment mechanism relative to the causal comparison. For both arm-specific finite-population means to be learned without extrapolation, every unit’s two relevant potential outcomes must each have a chance to be observed. Thus, for the treatment-control comparison, \[
0<\pi_i<1
\qquad\text{for every }i.
\] Under nondegenerate complete randomization, \(\pi_i=N_1/N\); under the common-probability Bernoulli design, \(\pi_i=p\). Notice that complete randomization satisfies this unit-level requirement even though it assigns probability zero to every vector with the wrong treated count. For more complicated exposures, the relevant requirement concerns the exposure contrasts defining the estimand—not an abstract rule that every assignment vector must be possible.

title: L01: Introduction
text:
Potential outcomes as missing data
Potential outcomes invite a missing-data reading: after assignment, one entry in each row of the science table is observed and the other is missing. More explicitly, the indicator that \(Y_i(1)\) is observed is \(Z_i\), while the indicator that \(Y_i(0)\) is observed is \(1-Z_i\). Rubin’s missing-data framework distinguishes mechanisms according to whether missingness depends on observed or unobserved values (Rubin 1976; Seaman et al. 2013). Very roughly:

MCAR: missingness is independent of observed and missing values.
MAR: conditional on observed information, missingness does not depend on the missing values.
MNAR: dependence on missing values remains after conditioning.

Under complete randomization, assignment probabilities do not depend on the values in the fixed science table. In that limited, design-based sense, the missingness pattern for each treatment-specific outcome resembles MCAR: which entry is revealed is randomized independently of the values themselves. The assignment indicators remain dependent across units because the treated count is fixed, so the analogy should not be read as a claim that every missingness indicator is independent. More importantly, causal inference requires the interventions and their potential outcomes to be well defined; generic missing-data notation does not supply that scientific content.

title: L01: Introduction
section: Random arm sizes under Bernoulli assignment
text:
Random arm sizes under Bernoulli assignment
Under i.i.d. Bernoulli assignment, \(N_1\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,p)\). The usual difference in means is undefined when \(N_1=0\) or \(N_1=N\). Conditional on any nondegenerate realized count \(N_1=n_1\), however,
\[
\mathbb P_Z(\mathbf Z=\mathbf z\mid N_1=n_1)
=\binom{N}{n_1}^{-1}
\qquad\text{when }\sum_i z_i=n_1.
\]
The conditional design is therefore complete randomization with \(n_1\) treated units, and the difference in means is conditionally design-unbiased. This does not make the ordinary difference in means unconditionally unbiased as a universally defined estimator: it still has no value on the two empty-arm events unless an extra convention is imposed. L02 introduces Horvitz–Thompson estimation, which uses the known assignment probabilities and remains defined and unbiased without conditioning on nondegeneracy.

title: L01: Introduction
section: Exact randomization variance under complete randomization
text:
Exact randomization variance under complete randomization
We now derive Neyman’s exact variance formula rather than simply state it. The calculation has three parts: find the randomization variance of each observed arm mean, find their covariance, and then combine those pieces. The covariance matters because complete randomization selects complementary treatment and control groups rather than two independent samples.
The difference in means varies across assignments because different units enter each arm. To describe that variation, define the finite-population variances
\[
S_z^2
=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\{Y_i(z)-\overline Y(z)\}^2,
\qquad
S_\tau^2
=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(\tau_i-\tau)^2.
\]
Here \(S_1^2\) and \(S_0^2\) are \(S_z^2\) evaluated at \(z=1\) and \(z=0\). All three variances are fixed features of the science table. The only randomness below comes from the assignment.

Center the science table and recall the design moments
It will help to work with outcomes centered around their finite-population means. For this derivation only, write
\[
a_i=Y_i(1)-\overline Y(1),
\qquad
b_i=Y_i(0)-\overline Y(0),
\]
so that \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_i b_i=0\). Also define the finite-population covariance between the two columns of the science table,
\[
S_{10}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N a_i b_i.
\]
Under complete randomization, exactly \(N_1\) of the \(N\) units are treated. A specified unit is treated with probability \(N_1/N\), so
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(Z_i)
=\frac{N_1}{N}\left(1-\frac{N_1}{N}\right)
=\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2}.
\]
For two distinct units \(i\) and \(j\), the probability that both are treated is
\[
\mathbb E_Z(Z_iZ_j)
=\frac{N_1}{N}\frac{N_1-1}{N-1}
=\frac{N_1(N_1-1)}{N(N-1)}.
\]
Subtracting \(\mathbb E_Z(Z_i)\mathbb E_Z(Z_j)\) gives
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_Z(Z_i,Z_j)
=-\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2(N-1)},
\qquad i\ne j.
\]
This negative covariance is the algebraic expression of sampling without replacement: once unit \(i\) occupies one of the fixed \(N_1\) treatment slots, there is one fewer slot available to unit \(j\). Treating the assignment indicators as independent would discard exactly the feature of complete randomization that produces the finite-population correction.


Variance of each arm mean
Centering the treated mean gives
\[
\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}}-\overline Y(1)
=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i a_i.
\]
The finite-population mean \(\overline Y(1)\) is fixed, so it does not affect the variance. Expanding the variance of the sum into its diagonal and off-diagonal pieces yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}})
&=\frac{1}{N_1^2}
\operatorname{Var}_Z\!\left(\sum_i Z_i a_i\right)\\
&=\frac{1}{N_1^2}
\left\{
\sum_i \operatorname{Var}_Z(Z_i)a_i^2
+\sum_{i\ne j}\operatorname{Cov}_Z(Z_i,Z_j)a_i a_j
\right\}\\
&=\frac{1}{N_1^2}
\left\{
\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2}\sum_i a_i^2
-\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2(N-1)}\sum_{i\ne j}a_i a_j
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here and below, \(\sum_{i\ne j}\) runs over ordered pairs of distinct units. Thus both \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) appear.
The off-diagonal sum is not a new unknown. Because the \(a_i\) are centered,
\[
0=\left(\sum_i a_i\right)^2
=\sum_i a_i^2+\sum_{i\ne j}a_i a_j,
\]
and hence \(\sum_{i\ne j}a_i a_j=-\sum_i a_i^2\). Substituting this identity, and using \(\sum_i a_i^2=(N-1)S_1^2\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}})
&=\frac{1}{N_1^2}\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2}
\left(1+\frac{1}{N-1}\right)\sum_i a_i^2\\
&=\frac{N_0}{NN_1}S_1^2
=\left(\frac{1}{N_1}-\frac{1}{N}\right)S_1^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The factor \(1/N_1-1/N\) is the usual sampling-without-replacement correction. By the same calculation, now treating the \(N_0\) control units as a simple random sample from the fixed \(Y_i(0)\) values,
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}})
=\left(\frac{1}{N_0}-\frac{1}{N}\right)S_0^2.
\]


Covariance between the arm means
The two arm means are built from complementary groups, so their covariance must be included. Centering the control mean makes that dependence visible:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}}-\overline Y(0)
&=\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_i(1-Z_i)b_i\\
&=-\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_i Z_i b_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality uses \(\sum_i b_i=0\). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_Z(\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}},\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}})
=-\frac{1}{N_1N_0}
\operatorname{Cov}_Z\!\left(\sum_iZ_i a_i,\sum_jZ_j b_j\right).
\]
Expand the covariance inside the last expression, again separating the terms with \(i=j\) from those with \(i\ne j\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}_Z\!\left(\sum_iZ_i a_i,\sum_jZ_j b_j\right)
&=\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2}\sum_i a_i b_i
-\frac{N_1N_0}{N^2(N-1)}\sum_{i\ne j}a_i b_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because both sets of outcomes are centered,
\[
0=\left(\sum_i a_i\right)\left(\sum_j b_j\right)
=\sum_i a_i b_i+\sum_{i\ne j}a_i b_j.
\]
Thus the off-diagonal sum is \(-\sum_i a_i b_i\). Using the definition of \(S_{10}\) then gives
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_Z\!\left(\sum_iZ_i a_i,\sum_jZ_j b_j\right)
=\frac{N_1N_0}{N}S_{10},
\]
and consequently
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_Z(\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}},\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}})
=-\frac{S_{10}}{N}.
\]
The minus sign comes from writing the centered control mean as a negative sum over treatment indicators. It does not imply that this covariance must be negative: its sign also depends on the finite-population covariance \(S_{10}\) between the two potential-outcome columns.


Assemble the pieces
Since \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}=\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}}-\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}})
&=\operatorname{Var}_Z(\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}})
+\operatorname{Var}_Z(\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}})
-2\operatorname{Cov}_Z(\overline Y_1^{\mathrm{obs}},\overline Y_0^{\mathrm{obs}})\\
&=\left(\frac{1}{N_1}-\frac{1}{N}\right)S_1^2
+\left(\frac{1}{N_0}-\frac{1}{N}\right)S_0^2
+\frac{2S_{10}}{N}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining step rewrites the covariance between the two columns in terms of treatment-effect heterogeneity. Since
\[
\tau_i-\tau
=\{Y_i(1)-\overline Y(1)\}-\{Y_i(0)-\overline Y(0)\}
=a_i-b_i,
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_\tau^2
&=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i(a_i-b_i)^2\\
&=S_1^2+S_0^2-2S_{10}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substituting \(2S_{10}=S_1^2+S_0^2-S_\tau^2\) into the preceding variance expression produces Neyman’s exact formula (Splawa-Neyman et al. 1990):
\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}})
=\frac{S_1^2}{N_1}+\frac{S_0^2}{N_0}-\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}
}.
\tag{4}\]
The first two terms are the arm-specific variance contributions before accounting for how the two potential outcomes are paired within units. The subtraction by \(S_\tau^2/N\) records that pairing. If every unit has the same treatment effect, then \(S_\tau^2=0\). With heterogeneous effects, \(S_\tau^2>0\), so the exact variance is smaller than \(S_1^2/N_1+S_0^2/N_0\). This comparison describes the terms in the displayed decomposition; it does not say that changing a science table to create more heterogeneous effects must improve precision, since \(S_1^2\) and \(S_0^2\) may change as well.
A check using the six-plot science table. Suppose three of the six plots are assigned to treatment. From the complete table,
\[
S_1^2=\frac{22}{15},
\qquad
S_0^2=\frac{37}{6},
\qquad
S_\tau^2=\frac{113}{30}.
\]
Neyman’s formula therefore gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}})
=\frac{22/15}{3}+\frac{37/6}{3}-\frac{113/30}{6}
=\frac{23}{12}.
\]
There are \(\binom{6}{3}=20\) possible balanced assignments. Computing the difference in means under each one and averaging its squared deviation from \(\tau=11/6\) gives the same \(23/12\).
The numerical agreement is a useful check on the algebra; the formula itself applies to any fixed science table under complete randomization.
We cannot generally identify \(S_\tau^2\) from the observed experiment. Its calculation requires knowing each pair \((Y_i(1),Y_i(0))\), yet randomization reveals only one member of each pair. Equivalently, the cross-column covariance \(S_{10}\) is unknown. By contrast, provided each arm contains at least two units, its observed outcomes let us estimate \(S_1^2\) and \(S_0^2\). Omitting the nonnegative \(S_\tau^2/N\) term therefore gives an upper bound on the exact variance; replacing \(S_1^2\) and \(S_0^2\) with observed within-arm sample variances produces Neyman’s conservative variance estimator, developed in L02.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
text:
From an unbiased estimator to an uncertainty statement
Download: Lecture PDF
Under complete randomization with fixed arm sizes \(N_1\) and \(N_0\), L01 established that
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}
=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NZ_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
-\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^N(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}
\]
is design-unbiased for the finite-population average treatment effect \(\tau\). Unbiasedness is a statement about the center of the estimator’s randomization distribution. It does not say how dispersed that distribution is.
For fixed potential outcomes, define the finite-population variances
\[
S_z^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N
\{Y_i(z)-\overline Y(z)\}^2,
\qquad
S_\tau^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(\tau_i-\tau)^2,
\]
where \(\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\). These are fixed features of the science table, not variances over a model for the outcomes. Neyman’s exact randomization variance is (Splawa-Neyman et al. 1990)
\[
V_Z
:=\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}})
=\frac{S_1^2}{N_1}+\frac{S_0^2}{N_0}-\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}.
\tag{1}\]
After assignment, the observed sample variance in arm \(z\), when \(N_z>1\), is
\[
s_z^2=\frac{1}{N_z-1}\sum_{i:Z_i=z}
\{Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-\overline Y_z^{\mathrm{obs}}\}^2.
\]
Keep three objects separate:
Because the individual effects are not jointly observed, \(S_\tau^2\) is generally unidentified. The Neyman estimator drops its negative contribution. Under complete randomization,
\[
\mathbb E_Z(\widehat V_N)-V_Z=\frac{S_\tau^2}{N}\ge 0,
\]
so it is conservative. When treatment effects are constant, \(S_\tau^2=0\) and \(\widehat V_N\) is unbiased for \(V_Z\); this does not mean that every realized variance estimate equals the true randomization variance.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
text:
The Bernoulli subtlety
With common Bernoulli probability \(p\), the usual difference in means divides by the random counts \(N_1\) and \(N_0\). It is undefined when either count is zero. Conditional on any \(N_1=n_1\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}\), however, the assignment is a complete randomization with \(n_1\) treated units. Hence
\[
\mathbb E_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}\mid N_1=n_1)=\tau.
\]
It is therefore conditionally unbiased on every nondegenerate arm size, but it is not an everywhere-defined, unconditionally unbiased estimator over the original Bernoulli design. By contrast,
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i
\left\{
\frac{Z_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{p}
-\frac{(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}}{1-p}
\right\}
\]
is defined and design-unbiased on the full assignment space.






NoteWhat HT is correcting



Inverse-probability weighting gives a unit that is rarely assigned to a particular treatment state more representation when that state occurs. The identity \(\mathbb E_Z(Z_i/\pi_i)=1\) is the entire unbiasedness argument for the treated potential-outcome mean. The cost is that small probabilities create large and noisy weights.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
section: A first variance comparison: HT versus Hájek
text:
A first variance comparison: HT versus Hájek
To see what normalization changes without carrying treatment and control notation through every line, isolate one generic finite-population mean under independent Bernoulli sampling. Let \(I_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)\) independently reveal fixed values \(Y_i\). The target total is \(T_Y=\sum_iY_i=N\mu\). Its inverse-probability estimate and the corresponding estimated population size are
\[
\widehat T_Y=\sum_i\frac{I_iY_i}{\pi_i},
\qquad
\widehat N=\sum_i\frac{I_i}{\pi_i},
\qquad
\mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_iY_i.
\]
This is the treated-arm problem with \(I_i=Z_i\) and \(Y_i=Y_i(1)\). For the control arm, take \(I_i=1-Z_i\), \(Y_i=Y_i(0)\), and replace \(\pi_i\) by \(1-\pi_i\). HT is \(\widehat T_Y/N\), whereas Hájek is \(\widehat T_Y/\widehat N\). Both numerators estimate the same total; only the denominator differs.
For HT, the estimation error has the exact representation
\[
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}-\mu
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i
\left(\frac{I_i}{\pi_i}-1\right)Y_i.
\]
Independence makes the cross-unit covariance terms vanish, giving the exact variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}})
=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_i\frac{1-\pi_i}{\pi_i}Y_i^2.
\tag{3}\]
Writing \(Y_i=(Y_i-\mu)+\mu\) separates two sources of error:
\[
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}}-\mu
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i
\left(\frac{I_i}{\pi_i}-1\right)(Y_i-\mu)
+\mu\left(\frac{\widehat N}{N}-1\right).
\tag{4}\]
The second term is produced by the random total weight. If the same constant \(a\) were added to every \(Y_i\), the target mean would increase by \(a\), but the HT estimation error would also acquire \(a(\widehat N/N-1)\). Thus HT variance can depend on the common additive baseline of the outcomes, not only on how dispersed they are around their mean.
When \(\widehat N>0\), Hájek divides by the realized total weight, so the same additive shift simply adds \(a\) to both the estimate and its target. Its estimation error is unchanged. The price is a random denominator, which makes an exact finite-sample variance less transparent.
The Taylor calculation shows how normalization removes the random-baseline term. Apply \(f(t,n)=t/n\) to \((\widehat T_Y,\widehat N)\) and expand around the expectations \((T_Y,N)=(N\mu,N)\). Because the two derivatives at that point are \(1/N\) and \(-\mu/N\),
\[
\frac{\widehat T_Y}{\widehat N}
\approx
\mu+\frac{\widehat T_Y-T_Y}{N}
-\frac{\mu}{N}(\widehat N-N).
\]
Substituting the two weighted totals and collecting each unit’s contribution gives
\[
\widehat\mu_{\mathrm H}-\mu
\approx
\frac{1}{N}\sum_i
\left(\frac{I_i}{\pi_i}-1\right)(Y_i-\mu).
\tag{5}\]
Consequently, its first-order variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm H})
\approx\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_i\frac{1-\pi_i}{\pi_i}(Y_i-\mu)^2.
\tag{6}\]
The contrast between Equation 3 and Equation 6 is now explicit: HT’s exact variance involves the squared outcomes \(Y_i^2\), whereas the first-order Hájek variance involves squared deviations \((Y_i-\mu)^2\). With common \(\pi_i=p\),
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{HT}})
-\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm H})
\approx \frac{1-p}{pN}\mu^2.
\]
The difference is large when the outcome mean is far from zero relative to the outcomes’ dispersion. Equivalently, a common additive shift changes HT’s variance because random total weight multiplies that shift, while it leaves the first-order Hájek variance unchanged. This is the classic survey-sampling linearization logic (Särndal et al. 1989, 1992). The calculation isolates one arm; for the treatment-effect estimator, the treated- and control-arm variances must also be combined with their design covariance.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
text:
Ratio bias from normalization
Variance is not the entire comparison. A second-order expansion gives the approximate ratio bias
\[
\operatorname{Bias}_Z(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm H})
\approx
\frac{\mu\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat N)
-\operatorname{Cov}_Z(\widehat T_Y,\widehat N)}{N^2}.
\]
Here
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat N)=\sum_i\frac{1-\pi_i}{\pi_i},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}_Z(\widehat T_Y,\widehat N)
=\sum_i\frac{1-\pi_i}{\pi_i}Y_i.
\]
The expression is informative even before it is evaluated: ratio bias appears when fluctuations in the estimated outcome total and the estimated population size do not line up as \(\mu\) times one another. For common \(\pi_i=p\), the two terms cancel. This agrees with the exact fact that, conditional on any positive realized sample size, the Hájek mean is the ordinary sample mean under simple random sampling. The Taylor calculations nevertheless remain approximations to an unconditional ratio problem whose denominator can be zero. They are most informative when \(\widehat N\) is concentrated near \(N\). With small effective samples, extreme probabilities, or influential units, higher-order terms can matter and neither estimator has a universal MSE advantage.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
section: HT versus Hájek in a finite population
text:
HT versus Hájek in a finite population
The demonstration uses
\[
Y_i(0)=b+\sigma x_i,
\qquad
Y_i(1)=b+\sigma x_i+\tau,
\]
with finite-population \(x_i\) centered at zero. The common baseline \(b\) shifts every potential outcome by the same amount, so it changes neither the individual treatment effects nor the ATE. For an HT arm mean, however, that shift adds the random error term \(b(\widehat N/N-1)\). Because Hájek divides by \(\widehat N\), the same shift simply adds \(b\) to its arm-mean estimate and does not change that estimate’s variance. When \(b=0\), this first-order shift-cancellation advantage disappears; the random Hájek denominator can then produce more conditional MSE than HT’s fixed denominator.


Change the sample size, assignment probability, baseline, effect, and outcome scale. The skipped share records Bernoulli assignments with an empty arm, so both estimators are compared on the same nondegenerate assignments. Because this comparison conditions on nonempty arms, HT’s unconditional design unbiasedness is not the explanation for any displayed advantage; the comparison isolates numerator and denominator noise on a common assignment set.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
section: GREG from a known baseline total
text:
GREG from a known baseline total
Suppose an online platform fixes a population of \(N\) accounts before an experiment. For every account it already knows \(X_i\), the number of active days during the preceding four weeks. The finite-population mean
\[
\overline X=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i
\]
is therefore known exactly before assignment. By contrast, \(Y_i(1)\), the experiment-period outcome under treatment, is observed only for treated accounts.
The treated accounts may happen to include unusually active users. Under complete randomization, for example, their pre-period mean might be \(4.8\) active days even though the full roster mean is \(4.0\). Randomization makes this discrepancy zero on average across assignments, but it is present in the experiment that actually occurred. If a prespecified relationship says that one additional pre-period active day predicts roughly two units of the experiment-period outcome, the \(0.8\)-day imbalance suggests about \(1.6\) units of chance inflation in the treated outcome mean.
The same idea extends to a vector of pretreatment covariates. Define its HT estimate within the treated arm,
\[
\widehat{\overline X}_{1,\mathrm{HT}}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\frac{Z_iX_i}{\pi_i},
\qquad
\mathbb E_Z\!\left(\widehat{\overline X}_{1,\mathrm{HT}}\right)
=\overline X.
\]
The discrepancy \(\overline X-\widehat{\overline X}_{1,\mathrm{HT}}\) is observable and has design expectation zero. If \(\beta\) converts covariate imbalance into predicted outcome imbalance, the natural correction is
\[
\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{GREG}}(\beta)
=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{HT}}
+(\overline X-\widehat{\overline X}_{1,\mathrm{HT}})^\top\beta.
\tag{15}\]
Under complete randomization, \(\widehat{\overline X}_{1,\mathrm{HT}}\) is simply the ordinary treated-arm covariate mean, so it is the \(4.8\) in the example. For a coefficient \(\beta\) fixed relative to assignment, Equation 15 is the generalized-difference, or regression-control, construction at the heart of GREG. Replacing \(\beta\) by a weighted regression estimate gives the usual generalized regression estimator (GREG) (Cassel et al. 1976). In the scalar example, \(\beta=2\) makes the correction \((4.0-4.8)2=-1.6\).
Writing \(m_1(x)=x^\top\beta\) gives an equivalent prediction-plus-residual form:
\[
\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{GREG}}(m_1)
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i m_1(X_i)
+\frac{1}{N}\sum_i\frac{Z_i}{\pi_i}
\{Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-m_1(X_i)\}.
\tag{16}\]
The two terms divide the work. The full roster supplies the average prediction, which can be computed without observing any experiment-period outcomes. Inverse-probability weighting is then applied only to the prediction errors among treated units. If an intercept is desired, augment \(X_i\) with a leading \(1\). Under unequal probabilities, correcting imbalance in that intercept is exactly a correction for \(\widehat N/N-1\); under complete randomization, the intercept is already balanced. For \(\beta\) fixed before assignment,
\[
\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{GREG}}(\beta)-\overline Y(1)
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i
\left(\frac{Z_i}{\pi_i}-1\right)
\{Y_i(1)-X_i^\top\beta\}.
\]
Exact design unbiasedness therefore does not require the linear prediction to be correct: misspecification changes the residuals, but the IPW correction still centers their contribution correctly. Under independent Bernoulli assignment, the exact variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z\{\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{GREG}}(\beta)\}
=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_i\frac{1-\pi_i}{\pi_i}
\{Y_i(1)-X_i^\top\beta\}^2.
\]
HT is the case \(\beta=0\). At the other extreme, if the prediction were exact for every unit, every residual would be zero and the treated potential-outcome mean could be recovered from full-roster predictions without assignment noise. Between those extremes, the fixed-coefficient estimator reduces variance when the chosen coefficient leaves less design-weighted residual variation than the raw outcomes; an arbitrary or poorly transported coefficient need not help.
For control, replace \(Z_i/\pi_i\) by \((1-Z_i)/(1-\pi_i)\) and use a control-outcome prediction \(m_0\). Subtracting the two prediction-plus-residual arm means estimates the ATE. This is the separate-arm version of the adjustment in Equation 14.
In practice, \(\beta\) is often fitted from the realized outcomes. Then the fixed-coefficient argument no longer establishes exact finite-sample unbiasedness. A coefficient fitted on historical data can be frozen before assignment; a coefficient fitted within the experiment needs the regression-adjustment qualifications discussed above. L03 uses the prediction-plus-IPW construction for both arms and names the resulting general form AIPW (Robins et al. 1994).

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
text:
CUPED: choosing the control coefficient
The same online setting provides a natural scalar control variable: the outcome metric measured before the experiment. In this subsection, take \(X_i\) to be that single pre-period metric rather than a vector. CUPED, short for controlled-experiment using pre-experiment data, transforms the observed outcome to
\[
Y_i^{\mathrm{cuped}}(\theta)
=Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-\theta(X_i-\overline X).
\]
Subtracting the same pretreatment quantity from \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\) does not change unit \(i\)’s treatment effect. Centering at \(\overline X\) makes the transformed outcome retain the original finite-population mean within each treatment state. Taking the difference in arm means therefore gives, equivalently,
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{CUPED}}(\theta)
=\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}-\theta\widehat\tau_X.
\tag{17}\]
Here \(\theta\) has the units of outcome per unit of the pre-period metric: it says how much outcome difference should be removed for one unit of chance covariate imbalance. For every \(\theta\) fixed before assignment, this estimator remains design-unbiased because \(\mathbb E_Z(\widehat\tau_X)=0\). The choice of \(\theta\) controls precision. Expanding the variance of \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}-\theta\widehat\tau_X\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}_Z\{\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{CUPED}}(\theta)\}
={}&\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}})
+\theta^2\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_X)\\
&-2\theta\operatorname{Cov}_Z
(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}},\widehat\tau_X).
\end{aligned}
\tag{18}\]
When \(\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_X)>0\), this quadratic is minimized at
\[
\theta^*
=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_Z
(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}},\widehat\tau_X)}
{\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_X)}.
\tag{19}\]
This is an oracle coefficient: its covariance with the treatment-effect estimator depends on the potential-outcome schedule and is not known before the experiment. At this value, the variance reduction relative to unadjusted difference in means is \(\operatorname{Cov}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}},\widehat\tau_X)^2/
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_X)\). Thus \(\theta\) should be near zero when the pre-period measure does not predict experiment-period outcomes, and a poor coefficient can increase rather than decrease variance.
Under complete randomization, define the finite-population variance and arm-specific outcome–covariate covariances by
\[
S_X^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i(X_i-\overline X)^2,
\qquad
S_{zX}=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_i
\{Y_i(z)-\overline Y(z)\}(X_i-\overline X).
\]
The complete-randomization covariance identities are
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_X)
=S_X^2\left(\frac{1}{N_1}+\frac{1}{N_0}\right),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Cov}_Z
(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}},\widehat\tau_X)
=\frac{S_{1X}}{N_1}+\frac{S_{0X}}{N_0}.
\]
The second expression has a plus sign because both \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}\) and \(\widehat\tau_X\) subtract their control-arm means. Substituting these identities into Equation 19 gives
\[
\theta^*
=\frac{S_{1X}/N_1+S_{0X}/N_0}
{S_X^2(1/N_1+1/N_0)}
=\frac{N_0}{N}\frac{S_{1X}}{S_X^2}
+\frac{N_1}{N}\frac{S_{0X}}{S_X^2}.
\]
The oracle coefficient is therefore an allocation-weighted average of the two arm-specific slopes, with each slope weighted by the size of the opposite arm. Under equal allocation it is their simple average; if the two slopes coincide, their common value is optimal for any allocation. This calculation explains both why a pooled slope can work well and why treatment-specific slopes can improve on it.
The original CUPED recommendation is to use the same metric from a nearby pre-experiment period: it is often strongly correlated with the experiment-period metric while remaining unaffected by treatment (Deng et al. 2013). There are several practical ways to choose \(\theta\):

Estimate it before the experiment. Use comparable historical experiments, a separate cohort, or relationships between earlier pretreatment windows, then freeze the coefficient before assignment. This preserves the exact fixed-coefficient design argument, but relies on stability across periods.
Estimate the oracle combination in the experiment. Estimate a slope within each arm, say \(\widehat\beta_1\) and \(\widehat\beta_0\), and combine them as \((N_0/N)\widehat\beta_1+(N_1/N)\widehat\beta_0\), mirroring the last expression for \(\theta^*\). In a balanced experiment this is the simple average. Regressing \(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\) on an intercept, \(Z_i\), and \(X_i-\overline X\) gives a familiar pooled common slope; including \(Z_i\) means that the slope is learned from within-arm outcome–covariate association rather than from the treatment/control mean difference. In a large balanced experiment it provides a convenient estimate of the same average when both arms inherit similar covariate dispersion; ordinary pooled regression need not reproduce the oracle weighting in an unbalanced experiment. Because the same outcomes choose the coefficient and estimate the effect, exact finite-sample unbiasedness is no longer automatic; inference should account for the fitted adjustment.
Allow treatment-specific slopes when warranted. Include \(Z_i(X_i-\overline X)\), or fit the two arm-specific slopes directly. A single common \(\theta\) can leave precision unused when the prognostic relationship differs by arm (Lin 2013).
Regularize or cross-fit richer adjustments. With many baseline variables or a flexible predictor, assess predictive performance out of sample and use sample splitting or cross-fitting to limit overfitting. Cross-fitting does not by itself guarantee exact design unbiasedness, especially under fixed-total assignment. Only pretreatment variables belong in the adjustment.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
section: Practical experimentation: errors larger than the standard error
text:
Practical experimentation: errors larger than the standard error
Large samples do not rescue a broken experiment. The practical program begins with Kohavi et al. (2007); Crook et al. (2009) then documents recurring failures in online controlled experiments: incorrect variance and power calculations, misleading percent-change intervals, bot traffic, instrumentation failures, ramp-up effects, and treatment/control populations that are not actually comparable. These are failures of measurement and implementation before they are failures of asymptotic approximation.
The replication evidence in Kohavi et al. (2026) adds a selection lesson. Eight large-scale tests of previously reported experimentation “patterns” had median samples in the millions and small minimum detectable effects, yet only two produced significant movement in the expected direction and one moved significantly in the opposite direction. The discrepancy is consistent with underpowered discovery studies, selective reporting, and the winner’s curse: conditional on being selected for a large estimate, a noisy estimate is likely exaggerated.
Practical discipline follows: establish sample-ratio and instrumentation checks, specify the primary metric and analysis before looking, ramp cautiously, report uncertainty in interpretable units, and replicate claims that will guide many future experiments.
crumbs: 4  L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
text:
The propensity-score paradox
Why estimate an assignment probability that the experimenter already knows? The efficiency-bound analysis of Hahn (1998) sets up the issue. In a semiparametric superpopulation setting, Hirano et al. (2003) show that inverse-probability estimators using an estimated propensity score can be more efficient than otherwise analogous estimators using the true propensity.
There is no information paradox. Common likelihood and series estimators of the propensity score satisfy empirical fitting equations that can also impose useful covariate-balance conditions. Those conditions create a projection or control-variate correction, much like Equation 13 and Equation 21; arbitrary propensity estimation need not impose the same balance. The estimated propensity is not better knowledge of the randomization device. It is a route to an estimator that exploits realized covariate balance. In a randomized experiment, it is clearer to describe the gain directly as covariate adjustment or calibration, while retaining the known design probabilities as the basis for identification and inference.

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
section: A short history of inverse-probability normalization
text:
A short history of inverse-probability normalization
Horvitz and Thompson used inverse inclusion probabilities to estimate finite-population totals exactly unbiasedly (Horvitz and Thompson 1952). Ratio estimation and Hájek normalization can trade finite-sample bias for stability; whether that trade is favorable depends on the design and finite population. Trotter and Tukey placed normalization on a continuum (Trotter and Tukey 1956), while Basu’s survey-sampling arguments exposed how formally unbiased estimators can behave poorly when they ignore structural information (Basu 1971).
The same ratio appears in importance sampling: self-normalized importance sampling is stable and invariant to an unknown normalizing constant, but biased in finite samples (Owen 2013). Counterfactual learning rediscovered the same practical tradeoff when propensities are highly variable (Swaminathan and Joachims 2015). Adaptive normalization makes the amount of normalization estimable and connects its fixed point to regression control (Khan and Ugander 2023). The recurring problem is not domain-specific: random weights carry useful correction and avoidable noise at the same time.
crumbs: 4  L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls

title: L02: Basic Estimators and Experimental Pitfalls
section: Choosing estimators across families of experiments
text:
Choosing estimators across families of experiments
Parikh et al. (2026) argue against choosing whichever estimator looks best inside a single realized trial. That practice turns estimator selection into another opportunity for overfitting. They instead use sample splitting across a family of randomized trials to compare estimators under a prespecified objective.
Their applications make the objective dependence concrete: weighted least squares performed best for inference-oriented criteria, while difference in means performed best for decision regret in the examined settings. The point is not a new universal winner. It is that “best estimator” is incomplete without a loss function, a relevant family of experiments, and a selection procedure separated from final evaluation.

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
Ten coin flips disguised as one thousand
Download: Lecture PDF
An experimental design is a probability distribution over complete assignment vectors, not merely a list of unit-level treatment probabilities. The distinction matters whenever assignments are dependent. As an extreme example, suppose \(N=1000\) units each have marginal treatment probability \(1/2\). Partition them into ten groups of one hundred and flip one fair coin per group. Every unit in a group receives the same assignment.
The marginal probabilities match i.i.d. Bernoulli assignment, but the design contains only ten independent random decisions. Let \(g=1,\ldots,10\) index the groups, let \(\mathcal I_g\) be the set of units in group \(g\), and let \(A_g\in\{0,1\}\) be the result of its coin flip. Thus \(Z_i=A_g\) whenever \(i\in\mathcal I_g\). With treatment probability \(1/2\), the observable HT estimator (Horvitz and Thompson 1952) can be written first using observed outcomes and then, by consistency, using the corresponding potential outcomes:
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N
\left\{2Z_iY_i^{\mathrm{obs}}-2(1-Z_i)Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}\right\}
=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N
\left\{2Z_iY_i(1)-2(1-Z_i)Y_i(0)\right\}.
\]
The second expression may look as though it uses both potential outcomes, but its assignment indicators select only the observed one: the \(Y_i(0)\) term vanishes for a treated unit and the \(Y_i(1)\) term vanishes for a control unit. Subtracting the fixed estimand and collecting units that share a coin gives the exact error representation
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}-\tau
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{g=1}^{10}(2A_g-1)
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_g}\{Y_i(1)+Y_i(0)\}.
\]
The inner sum is a fixed group total; all assignment randomness in that group is the single sign \(2A_g-1\). Independence of the ten signs therefore gives
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})
=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{g=1}^{10}
\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_g}\{Y_i(1)+Y_i(0)\}\right]^2.
\tag{1}\]
Under i.i.d. unit-level Bernoulli assignment, the corresponding variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}_Z(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})
=\frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\{Y_i(1)+Y_i(0)\}^2.
\tag{2}\]
The contrast between Equation 1 and Equation 2 is the location of the square. In the grouped design, outcomes are summed within a group and then squared, so the one hundred units sharing a coin move together. Under unit-level assignment, each unit contributes its own squared term.
Take the stark special case \(Y_i(1)=a\) and \(Y_i(0)=b\) for every unit. The grouped design has variance \((a+b)^2/10\). That is exactly the i.i.d. Bernoulli variance for ten units, not one thousand. I.i.d. Bernoulli assignment of all one thousand units has variance \((a+b)^2/1000\).
This exact equivalence is specific to HT in the example with constant potential outcomes. It partly reflects HT’s random total weight: conditional on at least one treated and one control group, difference in means is exactly \(a-b\) and has zero variance. With heterogeneous group totals, however, every estimator’s assignment variation still originates in only ten coin flips. The example therefore combines two lessons from L02 and L03: normalization matters, and dependence determines the effective source of randomization.
The point is not that dependence is always harmful. The positive dependence in this example makes many units move together. Negative dependence, by contrast, can force treatment and control counts or covariate totals to balance and thereby improve precision. What determines these properties is the joint distribution of the whole assignment vector \(\mathbf Z\), not the marginal probabilities considered one unit at a time.

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
Matched pairs
Matched pairs are the limiting case \(N_h=2\) and \(N_{1h}=1\). Suppose there are \(H=N/2\) pairs, and label the two units in pair \(h\) by \(a\) and \(b\). Let \(A_h=1\) when unit \(a\) is treated and \(A_h=0\) when unit \(b\) is treated. The signed observed difference
\[
D_h=(2A_h-1)\left(Y_{ha}^{\mathrm{obs}}-Y_{hb}^{\mathrm{obs}}\right)
\]
always means “treated outcome minus control outcome”: when \(A_h=1\), it is \(Y_{ha}^{\mathrm{obs}}-Y_{hb}^{\mathrm{obs}}\); when \(A_h=0\), the sign reverses. Its design expectation is the average of the two unit-level effects in pair \(h\). Consequently,
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{pair}}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^H D_h
\]
is design-unbiased for the finite-population ATE. Because each pair supplies only one treated and one control observation, there is no within-arm variance estimate inside a pair. Precision is instead learned from how the randomized contributions \(D_h\) vary across pairs.
Pairing can be powerful because assignment only decides which of two deliberately similar units is treated. If the matched units have similar potential outcomes under each arm, the two possible values of \(D_h\) are close, reducing its assignment variance. Pairing concentrates randomization locally: each pair has only two possible assignments, although assignments remain independent across pairs. Bai (2022) characterizes precision-optimal matched-pair designs, while Bai et al. (2022) develops inference that respects the pairing. Poor matches can lock in bad comparisons, and missing outcomes are especially damaging. Matching should therefore be based on pretreatment information chosen for prognostic value, not on an urge to balance every measured variable.
crumbs: 5  L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
What rerandomization buys
Let \(\mathbf 1_N\) denote the length-\(N\) vector of ones, so the treatment-control complement of \(\mathbf z\) is \(\mathbf 1_N-\mathbf z\). If the acceptance rule is symmetric—\(\mathbf z\) is accepted exactly when its complement is—then every accepted assignment has an equally likely accepted partner that reverses all arm labels. With equal arm sizes, each unit therefore retains marginal treatment probability \(1/2\), and difference in means remains design-unbiased. The joint assignment distribution has nevertheless changed: assignments with large \(M(\mathbf Z)\) now have probability zero. When the balanced covariates predict outcomes, removing those assignments can substantially reduce variance.
But the analysis must use the design that was actually run. An exact Fisher randomization test of a sharp null should sample from accepted assignments, not from all complete randomizations. Under the regularity conditions studied by Li et al. (2018), the usual Neyman normal interval calculated as if complete randomization had been used is asymptotically conservative; this is not a universal finite-sample statement.
The large-sample result of Li et al. (2018) explains the mechanism. Decompose the outcome variation into a component linearly associated with the balanced covariates and a residual component orthogonal to them. Under their regularity conditions, the difference-in-means fluctuation likewise separates into two independent pieces. The residual piece remains asymptotically Gaussian because the acceptance rule does not directly constrain it. The covariate-associated piece has a Gaussian limit truncated to the accepted balance region. Rerandomization therefore shrinks precisely the part of the estimator’s variation aligned with \(X\). The precision gain is larger when that part explains more of the outcome and when the threshold is more stringent. Li and Ding (2020) then studies how regression adjustment and rerandomization interact rather than treating design- and analysis-stage balance as substitutes.

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
Gram–Schmidt walk designs
The word discrepancy describes a signed imbalance. To see the connection to experiments, suppose the treatment and control arms have equal size and define the assignment sign \(s_i=2Z_i-1\), which is \(+1\) for treatment and \(-1\) for control. Then
\[
\widehat\tau_X
=\overline X_1^{\mathrm{obs}}-\overline X_0^{\mathrm{obs}}
=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N s_iX_i.
\]
Thus choosing signs that make the vector sum \(\sum_i s_iX_i\) small is exactly choosing an assignment with small covariate mean imbalance. Discrepancy theory studies how signs can be chosen so that many coordinates or other linear summaries remain small simultaneously. The norm used to judge the signed sum specifies which kinds of imbalance matter.
A purely discrepancy-minimizing algorithm might return one deterministic assignment. The Gram–Schmidt walk (GSW) instead turns a discrepancy-control procedure into a randomized assignment design (Harshaw et al. 2024). It generates the signs through a random walk while steering their covariate sum toward balance.
The design has a tuning parameter that governs how aggressively the walk prioritizes covariate balance relative to unconstrained randomization. At one extreme it behaves more like conventional random assignment; at the other it pushes harder to keep the linear discrepancy small. Crucially, it retains prescribed unit-level marginals, such as \(\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=1)=1/2\), while inducing dependence among assignments. The resulting guarantees concern design-based mean squared error over specified classes of outcome structure. This separates GSW from selecting a single best-looking assignment: its balance comes from a probability distribution over assignments, not from abandoning randomization.
The guarantee also states its own limitation: linear balance protects outcomes whose conditional mean is well represented by the chosen linear features. Cytrynbaum (2026) shows that uniformly approaching classical efficiency over broad smooth outcome classes becomes impossible once dimension grows too quickly. The paper develops a nonparametric, kernelized GSW in a reproducing-kernel Hilbert space and identifies more favorable rates under additive structure. Kernelization expands the function class being balanced; it does not eliminate the need to say which structure is plausible.
crumbs: 5  L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
section: Correlated cluster designs without rich covariates
text:
Correlated cluster designs without rich covariates
The paired-cluster discussion used covariates to decide which clusters should be compared. Candogan et al. (2024) ask a different question: can dependence be designed robustly when cluster size is the principal available structure? They study correlated cluster assignments with equal marginal treatment probabilities and a cluster-aware HT estimator, choosing dependence to minimize a worst-case variance criterion.
Their imbalance-reducing construction uses cluster sizes rather than a rich outcome-prediction model. The asymptotic guarantees require regularity, including that no single cluster dominate the population. The result is therefore neither covariate matching nor a claim that size is always the most prognostic variable. It shows that assignment correlation can be optimized against a stated worst-case class even when conventional matching information is sparse.
crumbs: 5  L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
section: Optimization-based designs and the value of randomness
text:
Optimization-based designs and the value of randomness
Once discrepancy has been written as a function of the assignment signs, one can search directly for the assignment minimizing it—for example, minimizing a norm of \(\sum_i s_iX_i\) subject to fixed arm sizes. Mixed-integer optimization can produce striking balance in small samples (Bertsimas et al. 2015), and minimax formulations connect classes of plausible outcome functions to the imbalance metric that should be optimized (Kallus 2018). The objective is never neutral: choosing a norm, feature map, or function class says which outcome patterns the design is intended to protect.
Selecting one minimizing assignment eliminates design-based randomization. Randomizing between that assignment and its treatment-control complement restores unit-level marginals of \(1/2\), but leaves only two assignments in the support. Either construction can be brittle to aspects of the outcome surface omitted from the objective. More diffuse randomization distributes that risk. Kallus (2021) formalizes this through mixed-strategy optimal designs: with no informative structure, complete randomization is minimax; gains require restrictions on plausible outcome functions, and inference supplies a reason to retain sufficiently diffuse randomization.
GSW, rerandomization, and mixed-strategy optimization occupy different points on the same frontier. Each asks how much imbalance to remove while preserving enough randomness for robustness and inference.
crumbs: 5  L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
Efron’s biased coin
Efron’s biased-coin design addresses a sequential problem: how can an experiment resist persistent arm-size imbalance without making its next assignment completely predictable? (Efron 1971) After \(n\) assignments, let \(D_n=N_{1n}-N_{0n}\) be the treated count minus the control count. If \(D_n=0\), assign the next unit by a fair coin. If \(D_n>0\), treatment is overrepresented, so assign the next unit to control with a chosen probability \(q>1/2\); if \(D_n<0\), assign it to treatment with that probability. The parameter \(q\) controls the pull back toward equal counts.
At \(q=1/2\), the feedback disappears and the rule is ordinary i.i.d. Bernoulli assignment. As \(q\) rises toward one, balance is restored more forcefully but future assignments become easier to predict. The design therefore makes the balance–randomness tradeoff explicit. Covariate-adaptive procedures such as Pocock and Simon (1975) generalize the same feedback idea to prognostic-factor imbalance, but the dependence created by that feedback must be reflected in the analysis.
crumbs: 5  L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
D-, A-, and E-optimal design
Section 7.5 of Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004) gives a modern convex-optimization treatment of a classical model-based design problem whose general theory traces to Kiefer (1959). Suppose measurement option \(r\) has a known regressor vector \(v_r\), and let \(\lambda_r\ge 0\) be the fraction of measurement effort allocated to that option, with \(\sum_r\lambda_r=1\). In a homoskedastic linear model, the normalized information matrix is
\[
\mathcal I(\lambda)=\sum_r\lambda_r v_rv_r^\top.
\]
When this matrix is nonsingular, the coefficient covariance is proportional to \(\mathcal I(\lambda)^{-1}\). The design problem chooses the allocation \(\lambda\) to make that covariance small, but a matrix is not ordered by a single universally best scalar. Common criteria emphasize different geometries:

D-optimality maximizes \(\det\{\mathcal I(\lambda)\}\), equivalently shrinking the volume of the coefficient confidence ellipsoid.
A-optimality minimizes \(\operatorname{tr}\{\mathcal I(\lambda)^{-1}\}\), the sum of the marginal coefficient-variance proxies.
E-optimality maximizes the smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathcal I(\lambda)\), protecting the least-informed coefficient direction.

These criteria are connected to covariate-balanced treatment design through convex optimization and worst-direction reasoning. They are not the same problem. Classical optimal design begins from a response model and chooses where to measure parameters; GSW chooses a randomized treatment allocation and seeks design-based protection over outcome classes. The analogy is most useful when it makes the assumed geometry explicit.
crumbs: 5  L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing

title: L03: Experimental Design, Blocking, Balancing
text:
Staggered rollouts beyond SUTVA
In a staggered rollout, clusters or units adopt treatment at different assigned times. The stepped-wedge formulation of Hussey and Hughes (2007) is a canonical example. The design creates comparisons across adoption cohorts and calendar periods. Operational constraints often motivate it, but the schedule can also generate deliberate variation in treatment saturation and exposure duration.
That variation is valuable when no-interference or no-carryover assumptions are implausible: outcomes can be indexed by neighbors’ adoption, local saturation, or time since treatment rather than by a single binary label. The cost is that calendar-time trends, anticipation, and dynamic effects become part of the estimand and design. A rollout is therefore not merely a delayed two-arm experiment; it requires a potential-outcome table indexed by assignment histories.

crumbs: 13  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Units, samples, and populations

\(N\) is the number of units in the finite experimental population, indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,N\).
\(X_i\) is the vector of pretreatment covariates for unit \(i\); \(\mathbf X\) collects these vectors.
A target population beyond the experimental units is described explicitly. Do not use “ATE” without making its target population clear.
crumbs: 13  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Treatments, assignments, and exposures

\(Z_i\in\{0,1\}\) is unit \(i\)’s treatment assignment, with \(1\) denoting treatment and \(0\) control. The assignment vector is \(\mathbf Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_N)\).
\(N_1=\sum_{i=1}^N Z_i\) and \(N_0=N-N_1\) are the realized treatment-arm sizes.
\(\mathcal Z\) is the support of the experimental design, the set of assignment vectors with positive probability.
When units are partitioned into \(H\) design strata or blocks, \(h=1,\ldots,H\) indexes the strata, \(N_h\) is the stratum size, and \(N_{1h}\) and \(N_{0h}\) are its treatment-arm sizes.
crumbs: 13  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Potential outcomes and observed outcomes

\(Y_i(z)\) is the potential outcome for unit \(i\) under treatment level \(z\in\{0,1\}\).
\(Y_i^{\mathrm{obs}}=Y_i(Z_i)=Z_iY_i(1)+(1-Z_i)Y_i(0)\) is the observed outcome when SUTVA and consistency hold.
\(\tau_i=Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\) is unit \(i\)’s treatment effect.
crumbs: 13  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Estimands and estimators

\(\overline Y(z)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i(z)\) is the finite-population mean potential outcome under treatment level \(z\).
\(\tau=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\tau_i=\overline Y(1)-\overline Y(0)\) is the finite-population average treatment effect. Qualify population and conditional versions with a subscript or argument, such as \(\tau_P\), \(\tau(x)\), or \(\tau_g\).
A hat denotes an estimator, a random function of the assignment and observed outcomes. Its value at the realized data is an estimate.
\(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{DM}}\) denotes the treated-minus-control difference in observed means.
\(\widehat\mu_{z,\mathrm{HT}}\) and \(\widehat\mu_{z,\mathrm{H}}\) denote, respectively, the Horvitz–Thompson and Hájek estimators of \(\overline Y(z)\). The corresponding treatment-effect estimators are \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{HT}}-
\widehat\mu_{0,\mathrm{HT}}\) and \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{H}}=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{H}}-
\widehat\mu_{0,\mathrm{H}}\).
\(\widehat\mu_\lambda\) denotes a member of the Trotter–Tukey affine normalization family, with Horvitz–Thompson at \(\lambda=0\) and Hájek at \(\lambda=1\). \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{AN}}\) denotes the adaptively normalized fixed-point estimator.
\(\overline X=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N X_i\) is the finite-population covariate mean. Center covariates at \(\overline X\) when writing regression-adjusted treatment effects.
\(\widehat\tau_X=\overline X_1^{\mathrm{obs}}-
\overline X_0^{\mathrm{obs}}\) denotes realized covariate mean imbalance.
\(m_z(x)\) denotes an outcome prediction for treatment arm \(z\); distinguish a function fixed before assignment from one fitted using realized outcomes.
\(\widehat\mu_{z,\mathrm{AIPW}}\) denotes the prediction-plus-IPW-correction estimator of \(\overline Y(z)\), and \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{AIPW}}=\widehat\mu_{1,\mathrm{AIPW}}-
\widehat\mu_{0,\mathrm{AIPW}}\).
crumbs: 13  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Assignment and sampling probabilities

\(\mathbb P_Z\), \(\mathbb E_Z\), \(\operatorname{Var}_Z\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}_Z\) refer to probability under the assignment design, holding the finite population and all potential outcomes fixed.
\(\pi_i=\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=1)\) is unit \(i\)’s marginal treatment probability.
When both treatment states appear symmetrically, use \(\pi_i(z)=\mathbb P_Z(Z_i=z)\), so that \(\pi_i(1)=\pi_i\) and \(\pi_i(0)=1-\pi_i\).
Use \(p\) for a common Bernoulli assignment probability.
crumbs: 13  Notation

title: Notation
text:
Finite-population and superpopulation operators

For \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(S_z^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\{Y_i(z)-\overline Y(z)\}^2\) is the finite-population variance of potential outcomes.
\(S_\tau^2=(N-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N(\tau_i-\tau)^2\) is the finite-population variance of unit-level treatment effects.
Within stratum \(h\), use \(\tau_h\), \(S_{zh}^2\), and \(S_{\tau h}^2\) for the stratum ATE and the corresponding finite-population variances.
\(s_z^2\) is the usual sample variance of observed outcomes within realized arm \(z\).
Unsubscripted probabilistic expectations such as \(\mathbb E\) refer to a stated superpopulation or statistical model, not to the assignment design.

Possible papers
The following papers are starting points rather than a closed list. They span the material in L01–L04 and vary in theoretical, computational, and empirical emphasis. In the proposal 1-pager, identify a tractable result, simulation, or empirical analysis to replicate and a specific extension or sensitivity analysis to investigate.

Randomization inference beyond the sharp null (L01). Caughey, Dafoe, Li, and Miratrix (2023), Randomisation Inference beyond the Sharp Null: Bounded Null Hypotheses and Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects. Reproduce one of the proposed tests or bounds, then study its finite-sample behavior, computational demands, or sensitivity to the assignment design.
Estimated propensity scores and efficiency (L02). Hirano, Imbens, and Ridder (2003), Efficient Estimation of Average Treatment Effects Using the Estimated Propensity Score. Reconstruct the paper’s efficiency comparison and investigate when estimating rather than inserting a known propensity score helps in finite samples.
Adaptive normalization of inverse-probability weights (L02). Khan and Ugander (2023), Adaptive Normalization for IPW Estimation. Replicate the comparisons among Horvitz–Thompson, Hájek, and adaptively normalized estimators, then alter the assignment design, outcome structure, or nuisance estimation method.
Regression adjustment in randomized experiments (L02–L03). Lin (2013), Agnostic Notes on Regression Adjustments to Experimental Data: Reexamining Freedman’s Critique. Reproduce a central simulation or empirical comparison and examine the role of treatment–covariate interactions, imbalance, or unequal treatment allocation.
Rerandomization (L03). Morgan and Rubin (2012), Rerandomization to Improve Covariate Balance in Experiments. Implement the design and reproduce its balance or precision gains, then vary the acceptance rule, balance metric, covariate dimension, or analysis procedure.
Algorithmic covariate balancing (L03). Harshaw, Sävje, Spielman, and Zhang (2024), Balancing Covariates in Randomized Experiments with the Gram–Schmidt Walk Design. Implement a manageable part of the design and compare its balance–randomness tradeoff with complete randomization or rerandomization.
Limited overlap and optimal trimming (L04). Crump, Hotz, Imbens, and Mitnik (2009), Dealing with Limited Overlap in Estimation of Average Treatment Effects. Reproduce the trimming rule and a key simulation, then examine how trimming changes both precision and the population whose effect is being estimated.
Smooth trimming and post-trimming inference (L04). Yang and Ding (2018), Asymptotic Inference of Causal Effects with Observational Studies Trimmed by the Estimated Propensity Scores. Compare hard trimming with smooth weighting and study bootstrap inference or uncertainty from the design stage.
Heteroscedasticity-aware trimming (L04). Khan and Ugander (2025), Doubly Robust and Heteroscedasticity-Aware Sample Trimming for Causal Inference. Replicate a simulation or application, then compare propensity-only and conditional-variance-aware trimming under alternative forms of heteroscedasticity.
Regularizing extrapolation (L04). Arbour, Parikh, Niknam, Stuart, Rudolph, and Feller (2025), Regularizing Extrapolation in Causal Inference. Implement the proposed regularization and investigate the paper’s bias–bias–variance tradeoff as overlap, dimension, or the outcome model changes.
